questions.question: Democracy comes from two ancient Greek words. Together, what do they mean?
questions.explanation: Demos means people and kratos means rule.
options: Rule by the people
Rule by one leader
Rule by the wealthy
Rule by judges

questions.question: In ancient Athens, eligible citizens voted directly on proposed laws. What is this system called?
questions.explanation: Citizens voting directly on laws is direct democracy. Australia mostly uses representative democracy.
options: Representative democracy
The separation of powers
Direct democracy
A federal system

questions.question: Who could take part in the democracy of ancient Athens?
questions.explanation: Women, enslaved people and people born outside Athens were excluded.
options: All adults living in Athens
Anyone who paid taxes in Athens
Free adult men who were citizens of Athens
All men and women born in Athens

questions.question: Which of these is an example of direct democracy in Australia today?
questions.explanation: In a referendum voters decide the question directly rather than through representatives.
options: A referendum on changing the Constitution
A federal election for the House of Representatives
A judge deciding a court case
Parliament voting on a new tax law

questions.question: A referendum needs a double majority to succeed. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: Both majorities are needed, which is why so few referendums succeed.
options: A majority in the House of Representatives and the Senate
More than half of voters in every state and territory
Two separate referendums with a Yes majority in each
A national majority of Yes votes and a Yes majority in at least four of the six states

questions.question: Since 1901, how many of the 45 proposed changes to the Constitution have been approved?
questions.explanation: Only 8 of 45 proposals have passed. The double majority is hard to achieve. The most recent referendum, in 2023, was the 45th proposal and it failed.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a modern democracy?
questions.explanation: A democracy needs a genuine choice of candidates and parties.
options: Free and fair elections
Equality before the law
Government accountability
One party chooses every candidate

questions.question: Journalists freely report on government mistakes and citizens can read their reports. Which feature of democracy is this?
questions.explanation: Citizens need information and the freedom to discuss it to make informed choices.
options: Equality before the law
Freedom of expression and access to information
The separation of powers
Compulsory voting

questions.question: In Australia, how can voters remove a government they are unhappy with?
questions.explanation: Elections allow power to change hands peacefully.
options: By voting for different representatives at the next election
By asking the High Court to dismiss it
By writing to the Governor-General
By holding a referendum

questions.question: Equality before the law means that...
questions.explanation: Nobody is above the law and nobody is beneath its protection.
options: the law applies to everyone in the same way, whatever their wealth or position
only citizens can be taken to court
judges must treat government leaders more harshly
everyone receives the same punishment for every offence

questions.question: What is the rule of law?
questions.explanation: The rule of law is broken when leaders place themselves above the law.
options: The police decide which laws apply
Laws only apply to citizens
Judges make all of the laws
Everyone, including government leaders, must follow the law

questions.question: When did the Australian Constitution come into effect?
questions.explanation: On 1 January 1901 the six colonies united to form the Commonwealth of Australia.
options: 11 November 1975
1 January 1970
1 January 1901
26 January 1788

questions.question: What happened in 1901 that created the Commonwealth of Australia?
questions.explanation: Federation joined the six colonies into one nation with a federal parliament.
options: The six colonies united under the Constitution
Australia became a republic
The first referendum was held
The states were divided into local councils

questions.question: What does it mean that Australia has a federal system?
questions.explanation: A federal system shares law-making power between national and state or territory governments.
options: Law-making power is divided between the federal and state or territory governments
All laws are made by one national parliament
Each state has its own Prime Minister
Local councils make most of the laws

questions.question: If a federal law and a state law conflict in an area where both can make laws, which one applies?
questions.explanation: Where both levels can make laws and they conflict, the federal law applies.
options: The state law
The federal law
Neither, until a referendum is held
The older law

questions.question: Which level of government establishes and supervises local councils?
questions.explanation: Local councils are the third level of government, but they are created and overseen by the states and territories.
options: The federal government
Local councils supervise themselves
State and territory governments
The High Court

questions.question: Why is law-making power divided between different levels of government in Australia?
questions.explanation: Dividing power also stops all government power being concentrated in one place.
options: National issues can be managed consistently while states and councils respond to local needs
So that every level makes exactly the same laws
To make sure elections are held every year
So that the federal government can control local councils directly

questions.question: Which level of government is mainly responsible for the defence of Australia?
questions.explanation: Defence affects the whole country, so it is a federal responsibility.
options: Local council
State government
Federal government

questions.question: Which level of government runs government schools?
questions.explanation: Government schools are run by state and territory governments.
options: Federal government
Local council
State government

questions.question: Which level of government issues Australian passports?
questions.explanation: Passports are a federal responsibility.
options: Federal government
State government
Local council

questions.question: Which level of government runs Victoria Police?
questions.explanation: Police forces are run by state and territory governments.
options: Local council
Federal government
State government

questions.question: Which level of government registers pets?
questions.explanation: Pet registration is a local council responsibility.
options: Federal government
Local council
State government

questions.question: Which level of government is responsible for immigration?
questions.explanation: Immigration affects the whole country, so it is federal.
options: Local council
Federal government
State government

questions.question: Which level of government runs trains, trams and buses in Victoria?
questions.explanation: Public transport is a state responsibility.
options: State government
Local council
Federal government

questions.question: Which level of government approves a permit to build a house extension?
questions.explanation: Building permits are handled by local councils.
options: Local council
State government
Federal government

questions.question: Which level of government is responsible for Australia's currency?
questions.explanation: Currency is a federal responsibility.
options: Federal government
Local council
State government

questions.question: Which level of government looks after a small neighbourhood park?
questions.explanation: Local parks are maintained by councils.
options: State government
Federal government
Local council

questions.question: Which level of government runs fire and emergency services?
questions.explanation: Emergency services are run by state and territory governments.
options: State government
Federal government
Local council

questions.question: Which issue should a resident raise with their local council rather than the state or federal government?
questions.explanation: Local parks and playgrounds are council responsibilities. Police and hospitals are state. Passports are federal.
options: A broken swing in the neighbourhood park
The number of police officers in Victoria
Staffing at a public hospital
A change to passport fees

questions.question: What is the separation of powers?
questions.explanation: Do not confuse it with the federal system, which divides power between levels of government.
options: Dividing government power between the legislature, executive and judiciary
Separating the Prime Minister from the Opposition
Dividing power between federal, state and local governments
Splitting Parliament into two houses

questions.question: Which branch of government makes and changes laws?
questions.explanation: Parliament is the legislature. It makes and changes laws.
options: Judiciary
Legislature (Parliament)
Executive government

questions.question: Which branch of government puts laws into action and runs government departments?
questions.explanation: The executive includes the Prime Minister, ministers and government departments.
options: Legislature (Parliament)
Judiciary
Executive government

questions.question: Who is part of the executive government?
questions.explanation: The executive puts laws into action and manages the day-to-day work of government.
options: The House of Representatives and the Senate
Voters and political parties
The Prime Minister, ministers and government departments
Judges and magistrates

questions.question: The federal Parliament is made up of...
questions.explanation: All three parts are needed for a bill to become law.
options: the Prime Minister and the High Court
the state premiers and local mayors
the Opposition and the crossbench only
the House of Representatives, the Senate and the King, represented by the Governor-General

questions.question: A government announces that judges must decide cases the way ministers tell them to. Why would this damage Australia's system of government?
questions.explanation: An independent judiciary is the part of the separation of powers that Australia keeps complete.
options: Elections would have to be held more often
Local councils would lose their powers
Parliament would no longer be able to pass laws
The judiciary would no longer be independent, so courts could not check the power of the government

questions.question: Which branch is at work when the Senate votes on a bill?
questions.explanation: Voting on bills is law-making, the job of Parliament.
options: Judiciary
Executive government
Legislature (Parliament)

questions.question: Which branch is at work when a government department starts paying a new benefit?
questions.explanation: Departments put laws into action, so this is the executive.
options: Legislature (Parliament)
Executive government
Judiciary

questions.question: Which branch is at work when the High Court decides whether a law follows the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Courts interpret and apply the law, including the Constitution.
options: Executive government
Legislature (Parliament)
Judiciary

questions.question: Which branch is at work when a minister directs a department to start a new program?
questions.explanation: Ministers and departments are the executive.
options: Legislature (Parliament)
Executive government
Judiciary

questions.question: Which branch is at work when a magistrate decides whether someone broke the law?
questions.explanation: Deciding cases is the judiciary's role.
options: Judiciary
Legislature (Parliament)
Executive government

questions.question: Which branch is at work when a parliamentary committee recommends changes to a proposed law?
questions.explanation: Committees are part of Parliament's law-making work.
options: Executive government
Legislature (Parliament)
Judiciary

questions.question: Which branch is at work when the Australian Federal Police investigate a suspected breach of federal law?
questions.explanation: Police enforce laws, which is part of putting laws into action.
options: Executive government
Legislature (Parliament)
Judiciary

questions.question: Which branch is at work when Parliament changes a law to strengthen environmental protection?
questions.explanation: Changing laws is the legislature's job.
options: Executive government
Judiciary
Legislature (Parliament)

questions.question: What is national identity?
questions.explanation: National identity is about belonging. Citizenship is a legal status.
options: The ideas, values, cultures and experiences that shape people's sense of belonging to a nation
A plan for addressing an issue
A person's formal legal membership of a country
The list of rights in the Constitution

questions.question: What is citizenship?
questions.explanation: Citizenship is a legal status that brings rights and responsibilities.
options: A feeling of belonging to a community
The right to live anywhere in the world
Membership of a political party
Formal legal membership of a country, with particular rights and responsibilities

questions.question: Maya feels strongly Australian but is not yet a citizen. Her brother is a citizen but says he feels more connected to the country where he was born. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Legal membership and a sense of belonging do not always go together.
options: National identity is decided by the government
A person must be a citizen to feel Australian
Citizens always feel more Australian than non-citizens
Citizenship and national identity are different things

questions.question: Which of these is a right of Australian citizens, rather than a responsibility?
questions.explanation: Rights include voting, standing for election, a passport and help overseas. Responsibilities include obeying laws, enrolling and voting, and jury service.
options: Applying for an Australian passport
Obeying Australian laws
Serving on a jury if selected
Enrolling to vote when eligible

questions.question: Which of these is a responsibility of Australian citizens?
questions.explanation: Jury service is a responsibility. The others are rights or privileges.
options: Receiving help from the Australian Government overseas
Applying for a passport
Standing for election
Serving on a jury if selected

questions.question: Which statement about voting in Australia is correct?
questions.explanation: Enrolling and voting is both a right and a responsibility of eligible citizens.
options: Eligible citizens must enrol and vote
Citizens vote directly on every law
Only members of political parties may vote
Voting is optional for citizens over 18

questions.question: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens promise to...
questions.explanation: The pledge reflects democratic values, rights, freedoms and the rule of law.
options: give up the traditions of their country of birth
join a political party and vote for it
serve in the Australian Defence Force
be loyal to Australia and its people, share its democratic beliefs, respect its rights and liberties, and obey its laws

questions.question: For at least how long have First Nations peoples lived on and cared for Country?
questions.explanation: First Nations peoples are the original inhabitants of Australia.
options: 10,000 years
40,000 years
65,000 years
2,000 years

questions.question: British colonisation of Australia began in...
questions.explanation: Colonisation began in 1788 and introduced British political, legal and cultural traditions.

questions.question: Which set of values is described as shared democratic values that connect many Australians?
questions.explanation: Shared values help people live together while keeping different cultural and religious identities.
options: Obedience, silence and tradition
Freedom, respect, fairness, equality of opportunity and a fair go
Wealth, power and competition
Loyalty to one political party

questions.question: Which of these is an example of civic action?
questions.explanation: Civic action is taken to influence an issue or improve the community.
options: Moving to another suburb
Watching a film about politics
Starting a petition about a local issue
Paying a parking fine

questions.question: What is civic action?
questions.explanation: Examples include petitions, contacting an MP, peaceful protest and contacting the media.
options: A law passed by Parliament
A vote held every four years
A court case about citizenship
An action taken by an individual or group to influence an issue or improve the community

questions.question: Which level of government should you contact about a plan to change the opening hours of your council library?
questions.explanation: Council libraries are run by local councils, so councillors are the right people to contact.
options: Local council
Your state Member of Parliament
The High Court
Your federal Member of Parliament

questions.question: A resident wants to oppose a federal plan to increase passport fees. Who is the best representative to contact?
questions.explanation: Match the action to the level of government that made the decision. Passports are federal.
options: A judge
Their federal Member of Parliament
Their state Member of Parliament
Their local councillor

questions.question: How is a law different from an ordinary rule?
questions.explanation: Laws are formal rules enforced by legal authorities.
options: A law can be enforced by legal authorities and breaking it can lead to a fine or imprisonment
A law can never be changed
A law is a suggestion rather than a requirement
A law only applies at school

questions.question: Which list gives the five characteristics of an effective law?
questions.explanation: An effective law balances certainty and change.
options: Popular, cheap, short, new, strict
Known, old, harsh, simple, federal
Fair, kind, stable, secret, clear
Reflects society's values, enforceable, known, clear and understood, stable

questions.question: A law reflects society's values when...
questions.explanation: People are more likely to respect laws that match their values. Laws may need to change when values change.
options: it has existed for more than 100 years
it matches the community's current beliefs about what is fair and acceptable
it is written by judges
most people have never heard of it

questions.question: A law is enforceable when...
questions.explanation: If a breach cannot be detected or punished, the law cannot be enforced.
options: authorities can identify when it has been broken and apply a consequence
it is published on a website
everyone agrees with it
it changes every year

questions.question: Why must a law be known?
questions.explanation: Governments communicate new laws through official websites, public information and the media.
options: So that it never has to change
So that judges can ignore it
People cannot follow a law they do not know exists
So that it only applies to adults

questions.question: Why must laws be stable but still able to change?
questions.explanation: Stability gives certainty. The ability to change keeps laws in step with society.
options: Laws should never change once they are passed
Laws should change every week to stay modern
Only the Constitution can ever change
People need certainty about what is legal, but laws must respond when society changes

questions.question: A council passes a new rule about where dogs may be off-leash but does not publish it anywhere. Owners are fined for breaking a rule they had never heard of. Which characteristic is missing?
questions.explanation: A law must be communicated before people can be expected to follow it.
options: Known
Enforceable
Stable
Clear and understood

questions.question: A state changes its e-scooter speed limit four times in one year. Riders no longer know what the limit is. Which characteristic is missing?
questions.explanation: Frequent change creates uncertainty about what is legal.
options: Reflects society's values
Stable
Enforceable
Known

questions.question: A 1950s law bans shops from opening on Sundays, but most people now shop on Sundays and the law is widely ignored. Which characteristic does the law now lack?
questions.explanation: Society's values have changed. Laws that no longer reflect them lose respect and may need to change.
options: Known
Reflects society's values
Stable
Clear and understood

questions.question: Which proposed law would be the hardest to enforce?
questions.explanation: Authorities cannot identify a breach of a rule about thoughts, so no consequence can be applied.
options: Drivers must not use a hand-held phone while driving
Households must put bins out by 6 am on collection day
Dogs must be on a leash in the main street
Everyone must think kind thoughts about their neighbours

questions.question: Which Australian state was the first place in the world to make seatbelts compulsory, and when?
questions.explanation: The road toll fell from 1,061 deaths in 1970 to 923 in 1971.
options: Victoria, 1901
Victoria, 1970
New South Wales, 1960
Queensland, 1985

questions.question: Some people opposed compulsory seatbelts at first, but wearing one is now widely accepted. What does this show about effective laws?
questions.explanation: The seatbelt law was clear, known, enforceable and stable, and society came to see it as reflecting its values.
options: Only federal laws are effective
Laws must never change
Unpopular laws can never be enforced
Laws and society's values can shape each other over time

questions.question: What does the principle of fairness mean in the legal system?
questions.explanation: Fair processes are impartial, consistent and give each side an opportunity to be heard.
options: Lawyers are free for everyone
Judges are elected by the people
Decisions are made through impartial processes and each side can present its case
Everyone gets the same result in court

questions.question: What does the principle of equality mean in the legal system?
questions.explanation: Equality means equal treatment and opportunity. Some people need extra support to achieve it.
options: Every case is heard by the same judge
The law applies to everyone in the same way, whatever their position
Everyone must have a lawyer
Only citizens can go to court

questions.question: What does the blindfold on Lady Justice represent?
questions.explanation: The blindfold stands for impartiality.
options: Courts are closed to the public
Evidence from both sides is weighed
Decisions are made without bias or favouritism
The law has authority to enforce decisions

questions.question: What do the scales held by Lady Justice represent?
questions.explanation: The scales stand for weighing both sides.
options: Evidence and arguments from both sides are carefully weighed
The cost of going to court
Decisions are made without bias
The law has authority to enforce decisions

questions.question: What does the sword held by Lady Justice represent?
questions.explanation: The sword stands for the authority to enforce.
options: The authority of the law to make and enforce decisions
Decisions are made without bias
Punishment is always severe
Evidence from both sides is weighed

questions.question: What is the difference between equality and equity?
questions.explanation: Equity can be needed to make equality real, for example an interpreter for someone who cannot follow proceedings in English.
options: Equality applies in courts; equity applies in Parliament
Equality is for citizens; equity is for visitors
Equality treats everyone the same; equity gives support according to need
There is no difference

questions.question: Which change would best improve access to justice for people in remote communities?
questions.explanation: Access improves when distance, cost, hours and delays stop being barriers.
options: Closing the nearest court to save money
Charging a fee to ask a legal question
A free legal advice phone line open outside school hours with short waiting times
Requiring all legal advice to be given in person in the city

questions.question: A magistrate realises the accused is her cousin and asks another magistrate to hear the case. Which principle is she protecting?
questions.explanation: Impartial decision-making is central to fairness. A personal connection could create bias.
options: Access
Stability
Known
Fairness

questions.question: What is a policy?
questions.explanation: Policies are plans, for example a plan to improve housing or transport.
options: A rule made by a court
A vote on changing the Constitution
A plan for addressing an issue or achieving a goal
An area of government responsibility

questions.question: What is a portfolio?
questions.explanation: Ministers are responsible for portfolios.
options: A party's campaign slogan
A list of candidates
A particular area of government responsibility, such as health or education
A seat in the Senate

questions.question: What is a coalition?
questions.explanation: A coalition can combine its seats to form government.
options: A party that wins every seat
The members who sit on the crossbench
Two or more parties agreeing to work together while remaining separate parties
A group of independents

questions.question: What is an independent?
questions.explanation: Independents decide their own position on each issue.
options: A candidate or member of Parliament who does not belong to a political party
A minister without a portfolio
A voter who has not enrolled
A judge of the High Court

questions.question: What is the crossbench?
questions.explanation: Minor-party members and independents usually sit on the crossbench.
options: Members of Parliament who belong to neither the government nor the Opposition
The leaders of the two largest parties
The bench where judges sit
The front row of government ministers

questions.question: Who forms the Opposition?
questions.explanation: The Opposition is the largest group outside government.
options: All of the independents
The Senate
The party with the fewest seats
The largest party or coalition in Parliament that is not in government

questions.question: The House of Representatives has 150 seats. How many members must support a party or coalition for it to form government?
questions.explanation: 76 is more than half of 150.
options: At least 75
At least 76
At least 100
All 150

questions.question: In which house is the Australian Government formed?
questions.explanation: Government is formed by the party or coalition with majority support in the House of Representatives.
options: The local council chamber
The High Court
The Senate
The House of Representatives

questions.question: Who usually becomes Prime Minister?
questions.explanation: Voters do not elect the Prime Minister directly.
options: The leader of the Opposition
The person chosen by the Governor-General alone
The candidate with the most votes nationally
The leader of the party or coalition that forms government

questions.question: What is a minority government?
questions.explanation: Crossbench support lets a party govern without a majority of its own.
options: A coalition of every party
A government formed by the smallest party
A government that loses a referendum
A government with fewer than half the seats that governs with support from crossbench members

questions.question: What is a hung parliament?
questions.explanation: After a hung parliament, a party may negotiate crossbench support to form a minority government.
options: A party wins every seat
No party or coalition has majority support after an election
The Senate rejects a law
Parliament has been suspended

questions.question: A party wins 75 of the 150 seats. Can it form a majority government on its own?
questions.explanation: Half is not a majority. It would need crossbench support or a coalition partner.
options: Yes, if its leader is popular
Yes, because 75 is the most seats
No, it needs at least 76 seats
No, it needs all 150 seats

questions.question: A headline says a party leader automatically becomes Prime Minister after winning the most seats. What is wrong with this claim?
questions.explanation: A party needs the support of at least 76 members to form government. Its leader then usually becomes Prime Minister.
options: A party must win every seat to form government
Only the Senate can choose the Prime Minister
Voters elect the Prime Minister directly
Winning the most seats is not the same as having majority support in the House of Representatives

questions.question: When were political parties first mentioned in the Australian Constitution?
questions.explanation: A 1977 referendum changed the rules for replacing senators who leave office early.

questions.question: What do members of the same political party usually do in Parliament?
questions.explanation: Party members usually vote together, which is why seat numbers matter so much.
options: Vote randomly on each issue
Only vote on the budget
Sit on the crossbench
Work and vote together

questions.question: Sam says Australia is a direct democracy because adults vote. Which reply best corrects Sam?
questions.explanation: Australia is a representative democracy. Citizens choose members of parliament, who make decisions and laws for them.
options: Adults in Australia vote only once, in the year they turn 18
Only members of parliament are allowed to vote in elections
Australians mostly vote for representatives, who then make laws on their behalf
Australians vote on every proposed law at their local council

questions.question: Club A lets every member vote on each new rule. Club B elects a committee to make the rules. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Voting on every rule yourself is direct democracy. Electing others to decide for you is representative democracy.
options: Both clubs work like a representative democracy
Club A works like a representative democracy and Club B like a direct democracy
Both clubs work like a direct democracy
Club A works like a direct democracy and Club B like a representative democracy

questions.question: After a new train line opens two years late, the state government publishes a report on what went wrong and the premier answers questions about it in Parliament. Which action would most weaken government accountability here?
questions.explanation: Accountability means leaders explain their decisions and face scrutiny. Hiding the report and dodging questions removes both.
options: Refusing to release the report and declining to answer questions
Publishing the report in full on a public website
Inviting journalists to the parliamentary debate
Holding an inquiry into the delays

questions.question: In the country of Velmora, elections are held every five years, but only one party is allowed on the ballot paper. Which feature of democracy is missing?
questions.explanation: Regular elections alone do not make a country democratic. Voters also need a real choice between candidates and parties.
options: A government for the whole country
A genuine choice of candidates and parties
An official list of people who can vote
Elections held at regular times

questions.question: Nordale holds elections every three years, has five parties, lets newspapers criticise the government and makes its president obey the courts. Which detail is the best evidence of the rule of law?
questions.explanation: The rule of law means everyone, including government leaders, must follow the law. The other details are evidence of different features.
options: Newspapers can criticise the government
Elections are held every three years
The president must obey the courts
Five parties contest elections

questions.question: Parliament wants to change the wording of the Australian Constitution. What must happen before the change can be made?
questions.explanation: The Constitution can only be changed by a referendum, which is a national vote on the proposed change.
options: Voters must approve the change at a referendum
Every local council must agree to the change
The High Court must vote in favour of the change
The Prime Minister must sign the change into law

questions.question: Which statement about the Australian Constitution is correct?
questions.explanation: The Constitution is the set of rules for how Australia is governed. It set up Parliament and kept many powers for the states.
options: It removed all powers from the states
It can be changed by the Prime Minister at any time
It was written to set up local councils
It established the Australian Parliament and outlined its powers

questions.question: A fast-growing suburb needs a new government secondary school. Which level of government is mainly responsible for building and running it?
questions.explanation: State and territory governments manage government schools, public hospitals, police and public transport.
options: Federal government
State government
Local council

questions.question: The footpath outside Zara's house is badly cracked and the street sign on her corner has fallen down. Which level of government should her family contact?
questions.explanation: Local councils look after local roads, footpaths, parks and rubbish collection for their community.
options: Federal government
State government
Local council

questions.question: Which option correctly matches each branch of government with its role?
questions.explanation: Parliament (the legislature) makes and changes laws. The executive puts them into action. The courts (the judiciary) interpret and apply them.
options: Legislature interprets laws, executive makes laws, judiciary puts laws into action
Legislature makes laws, executive puts laws into action, judiciary interprets and applies laws
Legislature makes laws, executive interprets laws, judiciary puts laws into action
Legislature puts laws into action, executive interprets laws, judiciary makes laws

questions.question: In the country of Dorvan, one leader writes the laws, runs the government departments and decides every court case. Why is this a problem?
questions.explanation: Australia divides power between three branches so no single person or group controls the whole system. Each branch can check the others.
options: All power sits with one person, so nobody can check how it is used
Power is shared between too many different people
The courts have become too independent of the leader
Parliament has too much power over the leader

questions.question: In Australia, the Prime Minister and ministers belong to two branches of government at the same time. Which two?
questions.explanation: Ministers are members of Parliament and also lead the executive government, so the separation is not complete. The judiciary stays independent.
options: The executive and the judiciary
The legislature and the judiciary
The legislature and the executive

questions.question: How has migration changed Australian society?
questions.explanation: People have migrated to Australia from across the world, making it a multicultural society. Ideas about national identity have changed as a result.
options: It ended the influence of British traditions on Australia
It stopped ideas about national identity from changing
It has meant that all Australians now share a single culture
It has made Australia a multicultural society with many cultures

questions.question: Which statement is about citizenship rather than national identity?
questions.explanation: Citizenship is formal legal membership of a country. National identity is a person's sense of connection and belonging.
options: Lena received her Australian citizenship certificate at a ceremony
Lena feels at home when her family watches the cricket together
Lena feels proud when Australian athletes win medals
Lena speaks Greek with her grandparents and English at school

questions.question: Australian citizens have rights and responsibilities. Which pair are both responsibilities?
questions.explanation: Responsibilities include obeying the law, enrolling and voting, and serving on a jury if selected. The other options are rights.
options: Applying for a passport and standing for election
Obeying the law and serving on a jury if selected
Applying for a passport and receiving help from the government overseas
Standing for election and receiving help from the government overseas

questions.question: Four students care about litter in their town. Which student has NOT taken civic action?
questions.explanation: Civic action is something a person or group does to influence an issue or improve the community.
options: Leo speaks about the problem at a community meeting
Mia complains to a friend and does nothing else
Jack signs a petition asking for more bins
Ava writes a letter to her local councillor

questions.question: Which source would give the most reliable information about why a council made a decision?
questions.explanation: Reliable information comes from sources that are official, dated and can be checked.
options: A comment from someone who was not at the meeting
A headline shared without the rest of the article
Meeting minutes published on the council website
A neighbour's guess about what the councillors were thinking

questions.question: A group wants to show the council how many residents share its worry about a dangerous road crossing. Which civic action is designed mainly for this?
questions.explanation: A petition gathers many names behind one request. It shows decision-makers the concern is widely shared, but it cannot force them to agree.
options: Reading the minutes of council meetings
Voting at the next council election
Writing one letter to a councillor
Collecting signatures on a petition

questions.question: Residents are worried about aircraft noise from an air force base. Defence is a federal responsibility. Who is the best representative to contact?
questions.explanation: Match the issue to the level of government responsible. Defence is federal, so a federal Member of Parliament can raise it.
options: Their federal Member of Parliament
Their state Member of Parliament
Their local councillor

questions.question: A new law about flying drones is announced in one small notice that almost nobody sees. Which characteristic of an effective law is missing?
questions.explanation: People need to know a law exists before they can follow it. Governments use websites, public information and the media to tell them.
options: Reflect society's values
Be enforceable
Be known
Be clear and understood
Be stable

questions.question: A law states that shops must close at a reasonable hour. Why would this law be hard to follow?
questions.explanation: A law should clearly explain what people can and cannot do. Vague words make a law hard to follow and enforce.
options: It is not stable, because it mentions a time of day
It is not clear, because people will disagree about what a reasonable hour is
It is not enforceable, because police never visit shops
It is not known, because few people go shopping

questions.question: A law bans people from humming a tune while they are alone at home. What is the main problem with this law?
questions.explanation: To be enforceable, authorities must be able to identify when a law is broken and apply a consequence.
options: It is not enforceable, because nobody could tell when it was broken
It is not known, because nobody listens to music at home
It is not stable, because popular tunes change every year
It is not clear, because nobody knows what a home is

questions.question: Smoking was once allowed inside Australian restaurants. As community attitudes to health changed, laws were introduced to ban it. What does this show?
questions.explanation: People are more likely to respect laws that reflect the community's current beliefs about what is fair and acceptable.
options: Laws only change when a referendum is held
Laws should never change once they are made
Laws do not need to reflect what the community thinks
Laws may need to change when society's values change

questions.question: A state changes the minimum age for a learner permit three times in two years. Which characteristic of an effective law does this break?
questions.explanation: Laws should not change so often that people become uncertain about what is legal.
options: Reflect society's values
Be enforceable
Be known
Be clear and understood
Be stable

questions.question: A draft law says fences between neighbours must not be too high. Which rewrite would make the law clearest and easiest to enforce?
questions.explanation: The best rewrite swaps a vague phrase for a limit that can be measured and checked. Vague laws are hard to follow and enforce.
options: Fences between neighbours must not be higher than two metres
Fences between neighbours should be a sensible height
Fences between neighbours must suit the look of the street
Fences between neighbours must not block too much sunlight

questions.question: Which situation goes against what the blindfold on Lady Justice stands for?
questions.explanation: The blindfold means decisions should be made without bias or favouritism.
options: A lawyer explains a law in plain language
A decision-maker favours one person because they are old friends
A judge listens carefully to both sides of a case
A court makes sure its decision is carried out

questions.question: In a dispute between two neighbours, the decision-maker listens to both people and looks at all the evidence before deciding. Which principle of justice is this?
questions.explanation: Fairness means legal processes are impartial and give each side an opportunity to be heard.
options: Fairness
Equality
Access

questions.question: A court office starts opening on Saturday mornings so that people who work all week can lodge forms and ask how the process works. Which principle of justice does this support most directly?
questions.explanation: Access means people can understand and use the legal system, whatever their circumstances. Longer opening hours remove a barrier.
options: Fairness
Equality
Access

questions.question: The owner of the largest company in town is caught speeding. The law is applied to her in the same way as to any other driver. Which principle of justice does this show?
questions.explanation: Equality means people receive equal treatment and the law applies to everyone, whatever their position.
options: Fairness
Equality
Access

questions.question: Tran receives a court letter written in complex legal language and cannot find anyone to explain it. Which principle of justice is most at risk?
questions.explanation: If people cannot understand their rights or the process, they cannot use the legal system properly. That is a problem of access.
options: Fairness
Equality
Access

questions.question: Three students of different heights are each given the same small step to reach a high shelf. The shortest student still cannot reach. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Equality treats everyone the same. It does not always give everyone a fair opportunity.
options: Fairness, because both sides were heard
Equity, because support was matched to each person's need
Access, because everyone could reach the shelf
Equality, because every student was given the same step

questions.question: A school gives a student with a broken wrist extra time to finish a written test. This is an example of...
questions.explanation: Equity means giving different levels of support according to need so that everyone has a fair opportunity.
options: equality, because every student gets the same time
bias, because one student is favoured unfairly
enforcement, because the school used its authority
equity, because support is matched to the student's need

questions.question: Which is a role of political parties in Australian democracy?
questions.explanation: Parties develop policies, choose candidates and campaign. Their aim is to have members elected so they can influence decisions and laws.
options: Running elections and counting all of the votes
Appointing the judges who sit on the High Court
Developing policies and choosing candidates for elections
Deciding the outcome of important court cases

questions.question: Which of these is a policy?
questions.explanation: A policy is a plan for addressing an issue or achieving a goal. Parties develop policies to win support from voters.
options: The person a party chooses to stand for election
A slogan printed on a party's posters
The area a party spokesperson looks after, such as Health
A party's plan to plant one million trees

questions.question: A party spokesperson looks after one area of responsibility, such as Health or Education. What is this area called?
questions.explanation: A portfolio is a particular area of government responsibility. When a party forms government, its spokesperson for an area usually becomes the minister for it.
options: A policy
A portfolio
A crossbench
A campaign

questions.question: In ancient Athens, eligible citizens attended an assembly. What did they do there?
questions.explanation: Athenian citizens voted on laws themselves. This is called direct democracy.
options: Voted only for the leader of the army
Chose judges to write the laws
Debated and voted directly on proposed laws
Elected representatives to make laws for them

questions.question: Why is Athenian democracy described as limited?
questions.explanation: Only free adult men who were citizens of Athens could participate, so most people living there had no say.
options: Only the richest citizen could suggest a new law
Laws were made by priests instead of citizens
Citizens were only allowed to vote once in their lives
Women, enslaved people and people born outside Athens could not take part

questions.question: Complete the sentence. A modern democracy offers voters a choice of candidates and...
questions.explanation: A choice of candidates and political parties gives voters a real decision to make at election time.
options: local councils
political parties
court cases
royal families

questions.question: A famous athlete and a school cleaner each break the same road rule, and a court gives them the same penalty. Which feature of democracy is this?
questions.explanation: Equality before the law means the law applies to everyone in the same way, whoever they are.
options: Equality before the law
A choice of candidates and parties
Opportunities for citizens to participate
Free and fair elections

questions.question: Which situation shows the rule of law in action?
questions.explanation: The rule of law means everyone, including government leaders, must follow the law and respect court decisions.
options: Police arrest a journalist for criticising the leader
A ruling party bans every other party from the election
A court rules against the government, and the government obeys
A president cancels a court case against a close friend

questions.question: How is a referendum different from the usual way decisions are made in Australia?
questions.explanation: A referendum is a national vote on a proposed change to the Constitution. Voters answer the question themselves.
options: Voters decide the question directly, not their representatives
It is decided by the Prime Minister and the High Court
Only members of parliament are allowed to vote in it
Only voters living in the largest state can take part

questions.question: A proposed change to the Constitution wins a majority of voters across Australia, but a majority in only three of the six states. What happens?
questions.explanation: A referendum needs a double majority. That means a national majority and a majority in at least four of the six states.
options: It passes, because three states is half of the states
It is sent to the High Court to decide
It passes, because most Australians voted Yes
It fails, because it also needs a majority of voters in at least four states

questions.question: Complete the sentence. On 1 January 1901 the six Australian colonies united to form...
questions.explanation: The Constitution came into effect on 1 January 1901, when the six colonies became one country.
options: the United Kingdom
the Commonwealth of Australia
the Australian Capital Territory
the High Court of Australia

questions.question: Which list contains only federal government responsibilities?
questions.explanation: The federal government manages issues that affect the whole country, such as defence, immigration, currency and international trade.
options: Immigration, local parks and public transport
Police, defence and rubbish collection
Defence, immigration and currency
Public hospitals, currency and pet registration

questions.question: Which area is a responsibility shared between the federal and state governments?
questions.explanation: Some responsibilities, including health and education, are shared between the federal and state governments.
options: Health
Currency
Defence
Rubbish collection

questions.question: The Department of Education sends new funding to schools as part of a program announced by a minister. Which branch of government is doing this work?
questions.explanation: Ministers and government departments are part of the executive, which puts laws and programs into action.
options: Legislature
Executive
Judiciary

questions.question: Who represents the King in the federal Parliament?
questions.explanation: The federal Parliament is made up of the House of Representatives, the Senate and the King, who is represented by the Governor-General.
options: The Prime Minister
The Chief Justice of the High Court
The Leader of the Opposition
The Governor-General

questions.question: Why is it important that judges are independent of Parliament and the executive government?
questions.explanation: The judiciary stays independent so that courts can make decisions fairly and act as a check on the other branches.
options: So judges can write new laws more quickly
So Parliament does not need to hold elections
So courts can decide cases fairly, without government interference
So ministers can choose the outcome of important cases

questions.question: British colonisation of Australia began in 1788. Which statement about its impact is accurate?
questions.explanation: Colonisation significantly changed the lives of First Nations peoples and introduced British traditions that still influence Australia.
options: It ended all connection between First Nations peoples and Country
It immediately gave every person in Australia the right to vote
It had little effect on the lives of the people who already lived here
It greatly changed the lives of First Nations peoples and brought British traditions

questions.question: What do successful applicants do at an Australian citizenship ceremony?
questions.explanation: Applicants usually pass a citizenship test first. At the ceremony they make the pledge and become citizens.
options: Vote in a federal election
Sit the citizenship test for the first time
Make the Australian citizenship pledge
Apply for a visa to stay in Australia

questions.question: Which person is an Australian citizen from birth?
questions.explanation: People born in Australia are citizens from birth when at least one parent is an Australian citizen or permanent resident.
options: A baby born in Australia whose mother is an Australian citizen
A tourist visiting Australia for one month
A student studying in Australia on a temporary visa
A person who has just applied to migrate to Australia

questions.question: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens promise to uphold and obey Australia's laws. Which idea does this reflect?
questions.explanation: Promising to uphold and obey the laws reflects the rule of law, where everyone must follow the law.
options: The double majority
The rule of law
Direct democracy
A choice of political parties

questions.question: Why should citizens gather information before they take civic action?
questions.explanation: Informed citizens can explain the issue clearly, understand other views and aim their action at the people who make the decision.
options: So they can keep the issue secret from other people
Because petitions are illegal without a report attached
Because only experts are allowed to contact a Member of Parliament
So their arguments are accurate and they contact the right decision-maker

questions.question: The local council plans to remove the Wattle Creek skate park to build a car park. Who should residents contact first?
questions.explanation: Contact the level of government that makes the decision. This plan belongs to the local council, so councillors are the people to persuade.
options: The Prime Minister
Their local councillors
Their federal Member of Parliament
The Governor-General

questions.question: A group wants as many local people as possible to learn about an issue. Which civic action is designed mainly for this?
questions.explanation: An awareness campaign spreads information widely, for example through posters, social media and local news.
options: Running an awareness campaign
Holding a meeting that nobody is told about
Sending one private email to a friend
Waiting until the next election

questions.question: Which statement about protest in a democracy is correct?
questions.explanation: Peaceful protest is one way citizens participate. It must stay peaceful and lawful to be an appropriate civic action.
options: Protests are only allowed during election campaigns
Only members of political parties are allowed to protest
Citizens can protest peacefully to show decision-makers how they feel
Protesters may damage property if the issue is important enough

questions.question: A campaign advertisement should include a clear call to action. Which of these is a call to action?
questions.explanation: A call to action tells people exactly what to do next and when.
options: Email your councillor before Friday
The council has nine members
The skate park opened ten years ago
Some people prefer car parks

questions.question: A strong civic action plan considers different perspectives. Which step helps a group do this?
questions.explanation: Understanding who is affected, including people who support the decision, makes a plan fairer and more persuasive.
options: Asking how to finish the task as quickly as possible
Asking how to stop other groups from having a say
Asking which slogan sounds the most exciting
Asking who would be affected and how each group might see the decision

questions.question: Why does citizen participation matter in a representative democracy?
questions.explanation: Representatives act on behalf of the people. Participation tells them what people need and helps hold them accountable.
options: Voting is the only way citizens are allowed to take part
Representatives decide better when they know what the community thinks
Representatives must always obey the largest protest
Laws cannot be changed once they have been made

questions.question: Which of these is a law rather than an ordinary rule?
questions.explanation: Laws are formal rules enforced by legal authorities. Breaking one can lead to a consequence such as a fine.
options: Drivers must stop at a red traffic light
Students must wear a hat outside at lunchtime
Family members take turns to wash the dishes
Players must shake hands after the game

questions.question: Complete the sentence. An effective law needs to balance certainty and...
questions.explanation: Laws should be clear and consistent, but still able to change when society or circumstances change.
options: secrecy
punishment
change
popularity

questions.question: Why did some people oppose compulsory seatbelt laws when they were first introduced?
questions.explanation: Some people saw the law as government interference. Today wearing a seatbelt is widely accepted as a normal responsibility.
options: They believed the law had been made by the courts, not Parliament
They believed the law would apply only to passengers in the back seat
They believed that seatbelts would make cars travel much faster
They believed the government should not control what people did in their cars

questions.question: Victoria's road toll fell from 1,061 deaths in 1970 to 923 in 1971, after seatbelts became compulsory. What does this evidence suggest?
questions.explanation: The fall in the road toll is evidence that the law worked. Seatbelts cut the risk of serious or fatal injury by about half.
options: The seatbelt law made no difference to road safety
The seatbelt law helped to reduce deaths on the road
Seatbelts were only worn by drivers in 1971
Fewer people owned cars in 1971 than in 1970

questions.question: Which option correctly matches each symbol of Lady Justice with its meaning?
questions.explanation: The blindfold stands for decisions without bias, the scales for weighing evidence from both sides, and the sword for the authority of the law.
options: Blindfold means no bias, scales mean weighing both sides, sword means authority to enforce
Blindfold means authority to enforce, scales mean no bias, sword means weighing both sides
Blindfold means weighing both sides, scales mean authority to enforce, sword means no bias
Blindfold means no bias, scales mean authority to enforce, sword means weighing both sides

questions.question: In a legal briefing, what is a finding?
questions.explanation: A finding is the conclusion reached after weighing the evidence, for example that justice was achieved, partly achieved or not achieved.
options: A question asked of a witness in court
The punishment given to a person who breaks the law
A new law suggested by a member of Parliament
The conclusion a legal team reaches after examining the evidence

questions.question: Which of these could a legal team use as evidence to support a finding?
questions.explanation: Evidence is information that can be checked, such as documents, photographs and witness statements. Opinions and rumours are not evidence.
options: A guess about what probably happened
A rumour that team members heard at school
A witness statement and photographs of what happened
The team's personal opinion of the people involved

questions.question: Put these steps in the correct order. 1 A party or coalition with majority support forms government. 2 Citizens vote in an election. 3 Parties choose candidates and campaign.
questions.explanation: Parties select candidates and campaign, citizens vote, and the party or coalition with majority support in the House of Representatives forms government.

questions.question: Do Australians vote directly for the Prime Minister?
questions.explanation: Government is formed in the House of Representatives. The leader of the party or coalition with majority support usually becomes Prime Minister.
options: Yes. Every voter fills in a separate ballot paper to choose the Prime Minister
Yes. The party leader with the most votes across Australia becomes Prime Minister
No. The Prime Minister is chosen by the judges of the High Court after the election
No. Voters elect local members, and the governing party's leader usually becomes Prime Minister

questions.explanation: Accountability means governments answer for their decisions. Losing office is the ultimate consequence.

terms.definition: A person who seeks to be elected to Parliament or another governing body.
An agreement between two or more political parties to work together while remaining separate parties.
The set of rules that establishes how Australia is governed and how government power is divided.
Members of Parliament who belong to neither the government nor the Opposition.
A system of government in which people have a say in how they are governed.
A system in which eligible citizens vote directly on laws or decisions.
The two majorities an Australian referendum needs to succeed: a national majority and a majority in at least four of the six states.
The branch of government that puts laws into action and manages the day-to-day work of government.
The level of government responsible for issues affecting Australia as a whole.
A system in which law-making power is divided between federal and state or territory governments.
The party or coalition with enough support in the House of Representatives to govern the country.
The representative of the King in Australia, who gives royal assent to laws passed by the federal Parliament.
The house of the Australian Parliament in which government is formed.
An election result in which no party or coalition has majority support.
A candidate or member of Parliament who does not belong to a political party.
The branch of government that interprets and applies laws through the courts.
The branch of government that makes and changes laws. In Australia, this is Parliament.
A governing body that makes decisions and provides services for a local community.
A government formed by a party or coalition holding more than half the seats in the House of Representatives.
A government that holds fewer than half the seats but has enough support from crossbench members to govern.
The largest political party or coalition in Parliament that is not part of the government.
The law-making body made up of elected representatives.
An organised group of people who share similar ideas about how the country should be governed.
A plan for addressing an issue or achieving a particular goal.
A particular area of government responsibility, such as health, education or defence.
A national vote on a proposed change to the Australian Constitution.
A system in which citizens elect representatives to make decisions and laws on their behalf.
The principle that everyone, including government leaders, must follow the law.
The division of government power between the legislature, executive and judiciary.
The level of government responsible for issues within a state or territory, such as schools, hospitals and police.
The requirement that governments explain their decisions and can be questioned and held responsible for them.
A person who is legally recognised as a member of a country.
Formal legal membership of a country, involving particular rights and responsibilities.
An action taken by an individual or group to influence an issue or improve the community.
The ideas, values, cultures and experiences that shape people’s sense of belonging to a nation.
Beliefs about what is important, fair or desirable.
A written request signed by many people and sent to a decision-maker to show support for a change.
The ability of people to understand and use the legal system, regardless of their circumstances.
A law that is clear, known, enforceable, stable and reflects society’s values.
Treating people equally and ensuring the law applies to everyone in the same way.
Providing different levels of support according to people’s needs so they can have a fair opportunity.
Making decisions through impartial processes and giving people a fair opportunity to present their case.
A formal rule that is made and enforced by legal authorities.
